name: Borealis-Tomb
description: Borealis-Tomb earns its name twice over: its skies burn with permanent aurora, curtains of violet and sickly green that ripple from pole to pole, fed by a magnetic field that instruments still cannot fully model. Beneath the light show lies a world of black glacier ice, cracked into pressure ridges and stained rust-red where ancient brine has erupted and frozen mid-splash. The toxic atmosphere—a chlorine-tinged brew—tints every horizon the color of old bruises.

The aurora never sleeps and never quite repeats itself; watchers describe it as the planet breathing. Sound carries in muffled layers through the dense air, dominated by the deep percussion of shifting ice sheets and an odd harmonic hum near the poles that seems to come from everywhere at once. Visitors find their compasses useless and their sense of direction dissolving within hours.

The magnetic anomalies are no accident of geology alone: they trace precisely to vast subglacial vent fields where superheated water pours into a buried ocean, feeding microbial ecosystems that thrive on chemistry instead of light. The colonies grow in chimney cities meters tall, biomass so dense that prospectors have already priced it as a resource. Decades ago, an automated beacon was planted in orbit to warn ships away from something—it still transmits a navigation hazard code, but the registry entry explaining what the hazard is was lost with the company that installed it.

Bio-extraction consortiums circle Borealis-Tomb like patient sharks, drawn by biomass yields that would end famine markets across three sectors. Survey crews, though, keep reporting equipment failures clustered around the southern vent fields, and one drilling platform returned with its crew unable to explain eleven missing hours. The old beacon's warning stands unanswered. Someone, eventually, will decide to switch it off—and that decision may matter more than anyone expects.
